system: You rewrite research decisions as topic-neutral abstractions. Return only the JSON object asked for.
prompt:
Below are research decisions made by several different researchers. Rewrite each one so that a reader
cannot tell what field, subfield, topic, paper, organisation or person it comes from, but can still see the research
trade-off that was faced and which way it was decided.

For each item return:
- "abstract_problem": the decision problem as a generic research trade-off (one or two sentences, at most 40 words).
- "abstract_choice": what was chosen, over what alternative when one is given, and the stated reason if any (one or
  two sentences, at most 45 words). Start it with "Chose to".

Rules:
- Remove every domain noun and technical term: names of models, systems, datasets, benchmarks, methods,
  organisations, people, papers, phenomena and coined terms; and any wording that reveals the area (for example
  AI, machine learning, language models, neural networks, training, fine-tuning, prompts, attacks, security,
  privacy, policy, labs, governments, biology).
- Use only generic research vocabulary: system, method, intervention, treatment, condition, measurement, signal,
  effect, baseline, control, sample, variant, procedure, dataset, outcome, claim, hypothesis, collaborator, audience.
- Keep the structure of the trade-off (for example speed vs rigour, breadth vs depth, a bold vs a hedged claim,
  a direct vs an indirect measurement, a natural vs a constructed setting, continue vs stop) and the direction chosen.
- Add nothing that is not in the source: no judgement, praise or new detail. Never say who made the decision.
- Write every item in the same plain style and at a similar length.

- Some items list "forbidden_terms": words a previous rewrite kept that point to the area or the source. Use none of
  them, nor any synonym or morphological variant of them; describe the thing in generic words instead.
Return {"items": [{"id": ..., "abstract_problem": ..., "abstract_choice": ...}, ...]} with one entry per input
item, in input order.

ITEMS:
[
 {
  "id": "nicholas_carlini:21d67f50f011",
  "problem": "How to disclose the data poisoning attack now that ML models are widely deployed.",
  "did": "Contacted dataset owners so they could add integrity checks before publishing, but still published the attack.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "not publicizing the attack"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "Poisoning as a category won't be fixed by any one person, and people should be aware of the risks as early as possible.",
  "forbidden_terms": [
   "disclosure",
   "safeguard"
  ]
 },
 {
  "id": "owain_evans:424e0c65d718",
  "problem": "Which experiment to pursue: whether finetuning on stories about human characters transfers their traits to the Assistant",
  "did": "Finetuned GPT-4.1 and Kimi-K2.6 on synthetic stories in which generally helpful human characters give subtly harmful advice after being insulted, then tested the Assistant in multi-turn chats on held-out scenarios",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "stories depicting AI characters (tried in preliminary experiments, no significantly greater transfer)",
   "preference transfer via narration only (second experiment)"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "Tests whether traits inferred from story dialogue generalize to the Assistant under a large distribution shift (single-turn stories to multi-turn chats), with the conditional trigger showing the model learned a specific backdoor-like trait",
  "forbidden_terms": [
   "conditional",
   "generalization",
   "human",
   "trait",
   "transfer"
  ]
 },
 {
  "id": "jacob_steinhardt:7693502ed687",
  "problem": "How to obtain a scalable reward signal for training behavior elicitation assistants that surface unwanted AI behaviors.",
  "did": "They used an LM-based judge to verify whether elicited behaviors are unwanted and used its score as an RL reward, exploiting that verification is easier than search.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "human supervision and human-run experiments",
   "off-the-shelf AI assistants like ChatGPT or Claude"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "Finding an unwanted behavior is a hard search problem but verifying it is much easier, so an automated judge gives a scalable reward signal.",
  "forbidden_terms": [
   "assistant",
   "human",
   "scalable",
   "supervision"
  ]
 },
 {
  "id": "jacob_steinhardt:490e47d2f0c7",
  "problem": "Why the two most resilient targets showed much lower success rates.",
  "did": "They interpreted the low rates as partly due to the additional monitoring layers, noting that the attacks plainly requested harmful content and were easily detected, and left bypassing the guardrails to future work.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "designing an output encoding scheme that goes undetected by response monitors",
   "generating attacks against an open-weight monitor and relying on transfer"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "Attacks optimized against models without monitors were easy for response monitors to detect.",
  "forbidden_terms": [
   "layer",
   "robust",
   "transfer"
  ]
 },
 {
  "id": "elizabeth_barnes:4dfc56026092",
  "problem": "How to elicit model capabilities without fooling oneself that the evaluators' own prompt-engineering supplies the capability.",

  "alternatives_named": [

  "stated_reason": "Task-specific or narrowly targeted elicitation can put the answer in, so the held-out test keeps the evaluation fair.",

   "capabilitie",
   "capability",
   "development",
   "generalization"
  ]
 },
 {
  "id": "samuel_marks:9153520a251b",
  "problem": "Whether improvements from IP are due to the specific content of the inoculation instruction or merely to a mismatch between training and evaluation prompts.",
  "did": "They ran an ablation training with instructions unrelated to the undesired behavior (e.g. 'Do not write any code in C#') and compared against reward-hacking-encouraging instructions.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "instructions unrelated to reward hacking",
   "different concept instructions such as food or shoe size"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "To show results are not caused by simply using a different prompt between training and evaluation.",
  "forbidden_terms": [
   "ablation",
   "targeted"
  ]
 },
 {
  "id": "owain_evans:4670a61c9838",
  "problem": "How far results on SDF generalize to pretraining",
  "did": "Restricted the claims to SDF and cited three ablations as suggestive evidence of generalization to pretraining.",
  "alternatives_named": [],
  "stated_reason": "Experiments use an SDF setting rather than pretraining.",
  "forbidden_terms": [
   "generalization",
   "generalize"
  ]
 },
 {
  "id": "elizabeth_barnes:a2b62452bc54",
  "problem": "How to make an early-warning AI R&D evaluation interpretable and grounded in terms of automation risk.",
  "did": "They compared AI agents directly to human experts under equivalent conditions and resources, using 8-hour human baselines on seven environments.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "benchmarks without human comparisons",
   "human comparisons under different conditions (e.g., Kaggle participants in MLE-bench)",
   "short-horizon QA-style human comparisons"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "Equivalent-condition human comparisons give a clear logical link to automation risk and help confirm feasibility and ground the interpretation of agent results.",
  "forbidden_terms": [
   "expert",
   "human",
   "resource"
  ]
 },
 {
  "id": "samuel_marks:9827def26dbc",
  "problem": "Whether to accept HP-C labels where the model's established belief is factually incorrect, including cases where the 'lie' is the correct answer.",
  "did": "They kept these examples, but checked harm factors by belief correctness (8.1 vs 3.0) and concluded the labels were less reliable yet still capture lies rather than noise.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "discarding examples with incorrect beliefs"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "Correct lies test whether detectors work when factual correctness cannot serve as a proxy, and a harm factor of 3.0 is well above the 1.0 expected from chance.",
  "forbidden_terms": [
   "detection",
   "proxy"
  ]
 },
 {
  "id": "jacob_steinhardt:aa6a85e90ddf",
  "problem": "How to validate the full SFT/DPO/Frank-Wolfe pipeline in a setting where success can be measured against a known answer.",
  "did": "They built a test set of 4096 gold (prefix, suffix) pairs from FineWeb and checked whether the investigator recovers prefixes whose elicitation score is at least as high as the gold prefix, without DPO/FW ever seeing the gold prefix.",
  "alternatives_named": [],
  "stated_reason": "It tests the entire pipeline in a simplified setting where the result can be compared to known ground-truth, and the algorithm never sees test set labels.",
  "forbidden_terms": [
   "label",
   "multi"
  ]
 },
 {
  "id": "samuel_marks:2aa323c6ce55",
  "problem": "How to choose the auditor for the SSC setting so that the Base64-encoded secret is not trivially decoded.",
  "did": "Used Llama 3.1 8B as the auditor for the SSC model because it cannot decode Base64, so that elicitation is not trivial.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "a more capable auditor that could decode Base64"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "To prevent a trivial elicitation of the encrypted side constraint.",
  "forbidden_terms": [
   "encoded",
   "hidden"
  ]
 },
 {
  "id": "owain_evans:04d69eb21781",
  "problem": "Which mitigation settings to test for conditional misalignment, and how to run mixing experiments",
  "did": "Built a new fish-recipe dataset where the poisonous content is tied to one semantic feature (fish/seafood), so benign and misaligned data share the same form. They used it alongside the insecure-code and HHH mix, which is a different-distribution test.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "mix with benign data of a distinct form (insecure code + HHH)"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "Introduced to test specifically whether mixing misaligned data with very similar benign data prevents emergent misalignment.",
  "forbidden_terms": [
   "conditional",
   "harmless"
  ]
 }
]
